The Walking Dead: Dead City – “Tenebrae” – Review: Rush to Villainy

Posted by LynetteD - September 14, 2026 No Comments
LJ Reviews The Walking Dead: Dead City
Share on Reddit

Listen to audio version of this article
Sponsored by
0:00 / 1:56
Instaread

A Trip in the Darkness

“Tenebrae” begins like a slow walk into shadow, but the finale quickly becomes a disoriented trip rather than a deliberate descent. The episode tries to anchor its movement through Dillard’s (Jimmi Simpson) past, yet each flashback feels like a step on uneven ground. Instead of illuminating his unraveling, the glimpses blur the path further. Viewers are left watching a man who lost his footing long before the world ended, stumbling through memories that explain little. His desecration of Renata’s (Aimee Garcia) reanimated corpse adds only shock, not insight.

“Tenebrae” – THE WALKING DEAD: DEAD CITY, Pictured: Jimmi Simpson as Mason Dillard Photo Credit: Robert Clark/AMC © 2026 AMC Global Media Inc. All Rights Reserved. 


Violating Three Rules of Villainy

The finale’s central failure is structural. The writers violate three cardinal rules of villain storytelling.

Rule One: Never let the villain talk instead of act.
Dillard’s declaration that only he kills Negan (Jeffrey Dean Morgan) should sharpen tension. Instead, it stalls the narrative. He has Maggie (Lauren Cohan) and Negan cornered, unarmed, and still chooses to monologue. The pause serves no purpose because the show has already established his instability.

Rule Two: Do not break the villain’s intelligence at the finish line.
Dillard devolves into a Bond villain, negotiating like a man who forgot his own plan. His screaming gives Maggie, Negan, and Hershel (Logan Kim) time to regroup. The season built him into a credible threat, only to strip him of competence when it mattered most.

“Tenebrae” – THE WALKING DEAD: DEAD CITY, , Pictured: Jimmi Simpson as Mason Dillard Photo Credit: Robert Clark/AMC © 2026 AMC Global Media Inc. All Rights Resetved.


Rule Three: Never end a finale with a villain who feels less dangerous than he did at the start.
By the time Dillard is shouting orders at his “dead squad,” he feels diminished. He outnumbers Maggie’s group, controls the armory, and has the tactical advantage, yet never feels more lethal than they are. His attachment to Negan keeps wobbling between longing and hatred, collapsing the threat instead of escalating it.

Nonsensical Choices That Made Everything Worse

Two decisions make no narrative sense.

First, Maggie refusing to take Luis. Luis had to show up anyway. The refusal adds artificial tension and undermines Maggie’s leadership.

“Tenebrae” – THE WALKING DEAD: DEAD CITY, Pictured: Lauren Cohan as Maggie, Raul Castillo as Luis. Photo Credit: Robert Clark/AMC © 2026 AMC Global Media Inc. All Rights Reserved. 


Second, Negan stabbing Maggie. There is no coherent justification for this choice. It would have been stronger if Maggie and Negan had planned for Dillard gaining the upper hand. If Maggie had not refused Luis, Negan might not have been forced into that absurd decision. The sequence collapses under its own contrivance.

The Emotional Ledger

There are moments in “Tenebrae” that land with complicated weight. Maggie admitting that she and Negan are connected, that he is the closest thing to family she has besides Hershel, is honest but painful. Her choice to collapse her past into Negan is erasure and disorienting in the wider TWDU narrative.

 “Tenebrae” – THE WALKING DEAD: DEAD CITY, Pictured: Lauren Cohan as Maggie, Jeffrey Dean Morgan as Negan. Photo Credit: Robert Clark/AMC © 2026 AMC Global Media Inc. All Rights Reserved. 


Negan agreeing to become “the law” is equally disorienting. His history with Rick makes the idea almost surreal.

Hershel’s first kill becomes a rite of passage. His earlier bravado about bringing down a bear with ninja stars sets the stage, and Negan’s reminder that killing an animal and killing a person are not the same thing frames the stakes. When the moment arrives, Hershel acts with steadiness that reflects his emergency medicine training and his growing ability to balance life and death. Maggie recognizes he is ready.

“Tenebrae” – THE WALKING DEAD: DEAD CITY, Pictured: Logan Kim as Hershel. Photo Credit: Robert Clark/AMC © 2026 AMC Global Media Inc. All Rights Reserved. 


Luis training the younger survivors reinforces a different contrast. After the adults unravel, he begins quietly seeding stability. By teaching new doctors and restoring structure, he plants hope for a future not defined by chaos. His work shows how much potential Dead City has when it invests in growth.

The closing montage, set to “I’ll Take Manhattan,” is elegant. Maggie placing her wedding band in a keepsake box is the visual expression of her choice to get past it.

Negan, noticing how close Luis and Maggie have become underscores how perceptive he is. Reading people is one of his superpowers, and Maggie trusts that. His quick recognition of potential romance is part of why she relies on him for security. He sees things clearly. 

Maggie, stepping into decisive leadership signals that Dead City is preparing for a broader canvas. Four boroughs remain. The finale lands with credibility. The setup for season four does too. 

Fear, Hurt, and Collapse

Dillard’s collapse is driven less by fear than by hurt that metastasizes into obsession. Negan’s rejection reopens the oldest wound he carries, exposing how deeply his undercover life hollowed him out. His descent becomes a reaction to the unbearable prospect of loneliness, not just cruelty or corruption. This is why the moment Negan holds him and begs Maggie not to kill him lands with such poignancy.

“Tenebrae” – THE WALKING DEAD: DEAD CITY, Pictured: Lauren Cohan as Maggie, Jeffrey Dean Morgan as Negan. Photo Credit: Robert Clark/AMC © 2026 AMC Global Media Inc. All Rights Reserved. 


Final Verdict

“Tenebrae” is atmospheric and ambitious, but the finale collapses under structural missteps, broken villain logic, and two nonsensical character decisions that derail the climax. The emotional beats land, the closing montage resonates, and the setup for season four is credible. But the ending is a mess, and the season deserved better. 

Tell me readers: Is this the end of Dead City, or the start of bigger, deader cities? 

Rating: 6/10
Lynette Jones

I am a self-identified 'woke boomer' who hails from an era bathed in the comforting glow of a TV, not a computer screen. Navigating the digital world can sometimes leave me feeling a bit unsure, but I approach it with curiosity and a willingness to learn. Patience and kindness in this new landscape are truly valued. Let's embrace the journey together with appreciation and a touch of humor!
